page.title: Delivery matrix
page.purpose: Answer the operator's first question — which iOS targets can I prove right now, what did the last run show, and what is standing between me and shipping this.

priorities.statement: Every target row shows a probed disposition, never an assumed one.
priorities.notes: A host being Linux does not imply anything except that the native iOS row is terminal. Every other row reflects what the last probe proved.

priorities.statement: A permanently unsupported row is visibly a different kind of answer from a blocked one.
priorities.notes: This ramp is the only one with rows that will never pass. Reading them as merely blocked sends the operator hunting for a fix that cannot exist.

priorities.statement: An unavailable target names its missing capability and next action inline.
priorities.notes: 'Unavailable' with no reason forces the operator into the CLI to find out why, which defeats the surface.

priorities.statement: The gate verdict and the release-readiness summary are both visible without navigating.
priorities.notes: The two axes are independent. A green matrix beside an unstarted ladder is the normal state, and hiding either one is how an owner discovers at upload time that they cannot publish.

priorities.statement: Wherever work executes remotely, the executing node is named.
priorities.notes: Remote execution is the normal path for this ramp. An unnamed remote failure is indistinguishable from a local one.

priorities.statement: A passing row carries the grade of the evidence that produced it.
priorities.notes: Two rows can both be green and mean different things. A pass produced by the pixel-grade mirror strategy cannot gate a release, and the matrix is where that has to be visible — it is the page the operator actually looks at.

elements.name: Target matrix
elements.description: One row per probed target: ramp, device kind, node, disposition, last run.

elements.name: Target disposition
elements.description: The closed-vocabulary disposition for one target row, carrying a text label as well as a status colour.

elements.name: Release gate
elements.description: The fail-closed gate verdict computed from the matrix.

elements.name: Release readiness
elements.description: Summary of the Apple readiness ladder, shown as a peer of the gate verdict rather than behind navigation.

elements.name: Executing node
elements.description: The bridge node that executed or would execute the cell.

elements.name: Generate project
elements.description: The primary action when no generated project exists yet.

elements.name: Evidence grade
elements.description: Whether the evidence behind a passing row was produced by a semantic strategy and can therefore gate a release, or by a pixel-grade strategy and cannot.

states.description: The matrix as the live system reports it, with a macOS node online.
Target inventory is being probed; no dispositions are asserted yet.
No generated project exists yet. Explains how to generate one rather than showing an empty table.
Targets are listed and at least one is unavailable — the normal working state, not a degraded one.
Dispositions are from a probe old enough that they may no longer hold; age is shown rather than the data being silently presented as current.
The inventory request failed. The matrix reports the failure rather than rendering an empty or all-unavailable table.
No macOS node is reachable. The native-Linux row is terminal and the simulator rows are blocked-but-fixable — two different answers shown side by side.
The fulfilling build host can still validate but can no longer produce submittable builds. The third category, and a dated one.
A required cell failed. The gate reads failed and names the contributing cell.
Every chapter passed, but the physical row was driven by the pixel-grade mirror strategy, so the row is green and non-promotable at the same time.

claims.statement: The release gate verdict and the release-readiness summary are both present on the matrix without navigating away.
claims.rationale: S2I-P0-010. Validation readiness and release readiness are independent axes. Collapsing them is how a fully passing matrix gets read as ready to ship.

claims.statement: Every verdict on this page is carried by the matrix and its disposition labels, so no recording has to be played to read it.
claims.rationale: Journey video is evidence, not interface.

claims.statement: Every state in which work executes on a node names that node.
claims.rationale: S2I-P0-004. Remote execution is this ramp's normal path; an unnamed remote failure is indistinguishable from a local one.

claims.statement: A validate-only host renders distinguishably from a fully capable one.
claims.rationale: S2I-P0-004. A host that can validate but not ship is a third category. An operator who cannot see it discovers it when an upload is rejected.

claims.statement: A matrix containing terminal rows renders distinguishably from one where every row is live.
claims.rationale: S2I-P0-003. The defining distinction of this ramp. If the two read the same, the operator cannot tell a missing machine from a category error.

claims.statement: The empty state presents the generate action rather than an empty table.
claims.rationale: An empty table is indistinguishable from a broken probe.

claims.statement: Every disposition is distinguishable without relying on hue — each carries a shape or text label as well as a status colour.
claims.rationale: DESIGN.md accessibility floor. 'unsupported' and 'unavailable' are semantically opposite — terminal versus actionable — and must not depend on colour discrimination to tell apart.

claims.statement: Every matrix row that carries a verdict also carries the grade of the evidence behind it.
claims.rationale: S2I-P0-010. Evidence grade is a property of a pass, not a footnote on the run page. Without it on the matrix, an operator reads promotable and non-promotable greens as the same result.

claims.statement: A matrix in which every row passed still renders distinguishably when one of those passes cannot gate a release.
claims.rationale: S2I-P0-010. This is the run-review promotability distinction propagated to the surface the operator reads first. If it stops at run review, the mirror strategy quietly manufactures shippable-looking results.
